analysis.one_liner: Creates a 500,000-worker agricultural guestworker visa with weaker wage and housing protections than the program it replaces.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill 20-16, and it was reported to the House floor in December 2014, but it never received a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The AG Act would replace the existing H-2A farm guestworker program with a new H-2C visa capped at 500,000 workers a year, run by the Department of Agriculture instead of the Labor Department. It sets the wage floor at the local prevailing wage rather than the higher special wage rate H-2A requires, drops the employer-provided housing requirement, and lets workers move between registered employers. It also bars most lawsuits for damages without 90 days of mediation, allows employers to require binding arbitration as a condition of employment, withholds 10% of each worker's wages until they leave the country, and denies these workers Obamacare subsidies and the child and earned income tax credits. It would let certain undocumented farmworkers gain temporary legal status, but only in this tied, temporary visa program.
analysis.who_benefits: Agricultural employers gain a much larger, faster guestworker pipeline with fewer wage, housing, and legal-liability obligations than the H-2A program they use today. Some undocumented farmworkers gain a route to legal work status, but only as tied temporary workers with no path to a green card.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual H-2C program at 500,000 workers, with emergency increases allowed for severe labor shortages, far above typical H-2A use.
Requires petitions to be approved or rejected within 10 business days and sets employer fees at $100 plus $10 per worker, capped at $1,000.
Lets workers who finish a contract move to any 'registered agricultural employer' on an at-will basis, and lets grower associations petition jointly for members.

Replaces H-2A's requirements with a wage floor of the greater of the local prevailing wage or the applicable minimum wage, and requires only transportation reimbursement and injury insurance, with no employer-provided housing.

Creates a legal work channel for aliens unlawfully present who performed at least 575 hours or 100 days of farm work in the prior two years, waiving grounds of inadmissibility so they can keep working in agriculture.

analysis.who_pays: Farmworkers, both U.S. and foreign: the wage floor is lower than H-2A's, the guest workers cannot bring spouses or children, 10% of their wages are withheld until they depart, employers can require binding arbitration, and lawsuits for damages need 90 days of mediation first. H-2C workers are also excluded from the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act and from ACA premium subsidies and refundable tax credits.

drawbacks.text: The wage floor is the local prevailing wage rather than the higher special wage rate H-2A requires, which labor advocates said would push down farmworker wages in areas with many guestworkers [S3].

The bill excludes H-2C workers from the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act, allows mandatory binding arbitration as a condition of employment, and requires 90 days of mediation before any worker can sue an employer for damages [S3].

No spouses or children may accompany H-2C workers, workers must remain outside the U.S. for set periods between contracts, and 10% of wages are withheld into a trust fund paid out only after the worker returns home [S3].

The status offered to undocumented farmworkers is temporary and tied to agricultural employment; it carries no path to permanent residence, and workers who lose their job have 30 days to find another or face removal [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a faster, larger labor supply to growers and a temporary legal channel to some long-present farmworkers, but the cost falls on the workers themselves: lower wage floors, no housing requirement, arbitration instead of court, no family accompaniment, and wages withheld until departure. An honest supporter would acknowledge that this trades worker protections for employer flexibility, and that the legal status offered is deliberately temporary.

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee approved it 20-16 in June 2013, reported it to the House floor on December 12, 2014, and placed it on the Union Calendar, but no floor vote ever came before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Goodlatte introduced the bill on April 26, 2013, and it was referred to the Judiciary, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means Committees.
A subcommittee hearing was held May 16, 2013, and the full Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported on a 20-16 vote on June 19, 2013.

The committee did not formally report the bill until December 12, 2014, when it was reported amended as H. Rept. 113-674, the other two committees were discharged, and it was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 506.
No floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farmworkers and their advocates are better off because the bill died: the higher-wage, housing-required H-2A program stayed in place instead of being replaced by the weaker H-2C program, and undocumented farmworkers were not pushed into tied temporary status.

for.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, brought it through his subcommittee and full committee, which approved it 20-16, and reported it to the House floor in December 2014.

for.name: 11 House cosponsors (10 Republicans, 1 Democrat)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the sole Democratic cosponsor later withdrew his name.

for.name: Agricultural employer groups
for.what_they_did: Backed expanding the agricultural guestworker program with lighter wage, housing, and litigation requirements than the existing H-2A rules.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote after it was placed on the Union Calendar in December 2014, and it died with the Congress.

against.name: Farmworker advocacy organizations
against.role: Groups representing migrant and seasonal farmworkers
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing its lower wage floor, exclusion from worker-protection law, mandatory arbitration, and no-family rule would leave farmworkers worse off than under H-2A.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only recorded vote was the 20-16 Judiciary Committee report, which came on the votes of the committee's Republican majority, and its cosponsors were 10 Republicans and just 1 Democrat, who later withdrew.

industries.note: The bill would give growers a 500,000-worker guestworker pipeline approved within 10 business days, with wages set by the local prevailing wage instead of H-2A's higher special rate, no housing obligation, and arbitration instead of lawsuits. Growers' gain in labor flexibility and cost comes at farmworkers' expense.

industries.industry: Farm labor contractors and joint-employer associations
industries.note: The bill lets associations file petitions and shuttle workers among member employers, with fines falling on individual members only in limited cases, expanding their middleman role in the farm labor market.

H-2C workers would be excluded from the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act, denied ACA subsidies and refundable tax credits, barred from bringing spouses or children, and required to arbitrate grievances and mediate 90 days before suing for damages.

The bill moves guestworker petition processing, investigations, audits, and penalties from the Labor Department to USDA, funded by employer fees, placing enforcement of farm labor rules inside the department most aligned with agriculture.
